description: We are a team of curious and creative students passionate about technology, robotics, AI, science, and innovation. We enjoy solving problems, learning independently, and turning ideas into real projects. We are looking for committed teammates with different skills who are willing to collaborate, share ideas, learn together, and build a functional solution.
summary:
We developed Argo-Twin, a digital twin prototype designed to help astronauts and mission control teams on Earth monitor crew health. The interface brings heart rate, body temperature, blood oxygen, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and radiation exposure into one dashboard. It also includes self-reported check-ins for mood and stress.

Argo-Twin L makes this information easy to review on computers, phones, and smartwatches. Its mobile view highlights readings that need attention and guides the crew through a simulated request for medical support when a critical alert appears. The prototype uses simulated data to demonstrate how real-time monitoring could work with compatible sensors.

In space, where access to medical care is limited, spotting health changes early can give crews and ground teams more time to respond. That matters for crew safety and for keeping future human space missions on track.
details:
Argo-Twin is an HTML prototype for a digital twin of a crew and habitat during a lunar or Martian mission. It brings physical and mental health indicators—such as vital signs, sleep, fatigue, mood, stress, and cognitive performance—together with habitat conditions in one interface.

The digital twin concept connects crew and habitat status so users can view indicators in context and explore how mission conditions may relate to changes in health and performance. The project is informed by NASA’s human-spaceflight hazards: radiation, altered gravity, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, and the challenges of a closed habitat.

The current prototype is an educational concept; it does not connect to live crew sensors or provide a validated physiological simulation. Example values should be treated as illustrative, not as real astronaut measurements.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Argo-Twin presents health and habitat indicators together, helping users understand how they may change over time and in response to mission conditions. Its intended impact is to support more human-centered planning for long-duration missions, when medical support and communication with Earth may be limited.

The project illustrates how a digital twin could help organize mission information and explore possible scenarios. It is not a deployed medical device, diagnostic system, or NASA-certified clinical protocol.

Tools and Technologies

- HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to build the interactive prototype.

- Obsidian and Markdown to organize research, notes, and project references.

- Obsidian Canvas and Mermaid to map relationships between hazards, health effects, evidence, and design questions.

- NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and NASA Human Research Program materials to research spaceflight health risks and studies.

- Canadian Space Agency resources for context on space science and radiation monitoring.

- Tailwind CSS, Three.js, D3.js, and Google Fonts for the prototype’s interface, visualizations, and typography.

Creativity and Design Considerations

Argo-Twin brings crew health, mental well-being, cognitive performance, and habitat conditions into a single digital-twin concept. The design considers mission duration, radiation, altered gravity, isolation, delayed communication, limited medical support, sleep, workload, and health-data privacy.

It distinguishes research findings, general reference values, and design ideas. Terrestrial reference ranges are not astronaut-specific clinical limits and should not be applied directly to lunar or Martian conditions.
